title: What We Mean by Teaching Reading
brief: Open by establishing that reading is one of the two receptive primary language skills (alongside listening), as defined in the module's module vocabulary and module focus section. Explain that receptive does not mean passive: the module shows students actively filling out worksheets, writing questions, and keeping vocabulary lists while someone else reads aloud, all of which count as engaged reading work. Use the module's plain distinction between primary skills and sub-skills (vocabulary, spelling) to frame what a reading lesson is actually developing. Close by noting the module's stated goal that skills should ultimately be used together for communication, while signalling that this unit focuses on the reading thread specifically.

title: Top-Down and Bottom-Up Processing in Plain Terms
brief: Explain bottom-up processing accurately as the skilled decoding of letters, spelling patterns, words, and phrases while meaning is built from smaller units upward; state explicitly that it is necessary reading work, not rote memorization. Then use the module's description of students choosing their own picture topics from magazines and writing about something of personal interest to illustrate top-down processing: readers bring prior knowledge, interest, and purpose to a text and use those resources to interpret the whole. Use the module's 'free write' activity, where one student already knew about bears from previous writing, to show how background knowledge shapes comprehension. Emphasize that fluent comprehension normally coordinates both processes rather than choosing one.

title: Choosing Texts That Work
brief: Use the module's definition of 'authentic' — tasks, activities, and materials used in real life by native speakers for actual communicative needs — as the starting criterion for text selection. Walk through the range of text types the module mentions: magazine pictures with captions, student-authored stories, library books and magazines, e-mails, web pages, poems, and journal entries from the iEARN projects. Highlight the module's point that authentic materials can be used in simulated classroom situations, and that student-chosen topics (cutting a picture from a magazine) give learners a stake in the content. Note the module's observation that students in the iEARN classes were of mixed age, grade, and ability levels, so text choice must allow for that range. Conclude with the module's practical note that internet resources are not always available and that print-based library materials serve the same purpose.

title: Staging a Reading Lesson: Pre-, While-, and Post-Reading
brief: Structure this section around the three-stage framework visible in the module's integrated-skills lesson. For pre-reading, draw on the module's use of brainstorming (defined as suggesting many ideas quickly in preparation for a future activity) and the 'Before Viewing' warm-up technique of asking learners to recall a scene they felt strongly about — adapted here as a way to activate prior knowledge before a text. For while-reading, use the module's 'active listening/reading' techniques: filling out a worksheet about the reading, keeping a list of unknown vocabulary, and writing one or two questions for the reader to answer afterward. For post-reading, draw on the module's follow-up suggestions: using the writing as stimulus for conversation, writing two questions to ask the class about content, and taking the text home for a longer assignment. Show how each stage serves a distinct purpose without reducing reading to a test.

title: Reading Tasks That Check Comprehension Without Killing Interest
brief: Focus on the module's principle that student choice and authentic purpose sustain motivation. Use the free-write activity as the central example: students chose their own picture, wrote about something personally interesting, and then read aloud while a partner completed a response worksheet — comprehension was checked through the worksheet and follow-up questions rather than a formal test. Introduce the module's 'jigsaw' reading technique from the iEARN Good Deeds project, where students divided into two groups to read different library materials and then combined their information, as a task-based comprehension structure. Mention graphic organizers (defined in the module as visual maps such as graphs, semantic webs, timelines, and story maps) as tools that help learners understand and retain information after reading. Close with the module's reminder that displaying student writing on walls or doors so others can read it turns comprehension into a real communicative act.

title: Adapting Reading Activities for Different Class Sizes and Contexts
brief: Use the module's explicit guidance on scaling the free-write and read-aloud activity from a two-student pair to a larger class: placing magazines in multiple locations, having students practice reading in pairs before performing for a larger group, and requiring active-listener groups to prepare a question for the reader. Introduce the chain-story (co-authoring in groups of three or four, passing the story around so every student writes a beginning, middle, and end) as a reading-and-writing task the module describes as working well with all ages and motivating participation. Note the module's content-based instruction definition — structuring lessons around central themes or topics — as a way to give a series of reading texts coherence across a unit. End with the module's practical note that exchange projects and authentic reading tasks can run entirely by post or with print materials when internet access is unavailable, reinforcing that the principles apply regardless of resources.
